name: State-dependent memory
statement: Memory is better when the place, drug state or mood at retrieval matches the one at learning, an effect that is small on average and largely absent from recognition tests.
meaning: Three separate literatures travel under one heading, and they are not equally strong. Environmental context-dependent memory asks whether changing rooms costs you anything. Drug state-dependent retrieval asks whether material learned drunk or sedated comes back best in the same state. Mood-dependent memory asks the same about happiness and sadness. All three share a mechanism: features of the learning episode get encoded alongside the target and can act as retrieval cues later. The shared claim is therefore about cues, not about storage. Nothing is lost when the context changes; what changes is how easy it is to find. That framing predicts the boundary condition that runs through all three literatures. A free-recall test gives the rememberer almost nothing to work with, so incidental cues matter. A recognition test hands back the item itself, and the effect mostly disappears.

origin.who: Duncan R. Godden and Alan D. Baddeley
origin.note: The paper is "Context-dependent memory in two natural environments: on land and underwater", volume 66, pages 325 to 331. Eighteen members of a university diving club were tested and the design ran on sixteen, two having been dropped for technical failures and replaced by another pair. Divers heard 36-word lists by underwater telephone on dry land or at about 20 feet in open water near Oban, and recalled them in the same or the other environment. Lists learnt underwater were best recalled underwater. A second experiment made divers enter the water during the delay and return to land to recall, and found no cost, which rules out disruption as the explanation. It was not the first such study. Smith and Vela date experimental work on environmental context to Carr in 1925, on maze running in rats, and their meta-analysis covers human studies conducted between 1935 and 1997. The diving study earned its place by making the context change as large as an experiment plausibly can.

evidence: Godden and Baddeley print four condition means in words recalled. Learning and recall both dry gave 13.5, SD 5.8; dry then wet gave 8.6, SD 3.0; wet then dry gave 8.4, SD 3.3; wet then wet gave 11.4, SD 5.0. Neither the environment of learning nor that of recall produced a significant main effect, and the interaction did, F = 22.0, d.f. = 1, 12, P < 0.001. Murre took that F and estimated eta squared as 22.0/(22.0 + 12) = 0.647, derived from it a lower bound of Cohen's d = 2.708, and judged sixteen divers enough for his own attempt. Smith and Vela's meta-analysis codes the same study at d = +0.91, 95% CI [-0.06, +1.88], an interval that includes zero. Godden and Baddeley followed it in 1980 with "When does context influence recognition memory?", British Journal of Psychology 71, pages 99 to 104. Subjects learned lists of 36 words on land or underwater and then tried to pick them out of a list of 72 words, in the same environment or the other one. Their abstract records the outcome as "no trace of context dependency was observed". Smith and Vela code that study at d = 0.00, 95% CI [-1.13, +1.13]. The pooled picture comes from Smith and Vela, who calculated 93 effect sizes from 75 studies in 41 articles conducted between 1935 and 1997. The average weighted effect was d = .28, 95% CI ±.05, reliably above zero, with substantial heterogeneity, Q_T = 242.47, p < .001. Moderators explain more than the average does. First-order reinstatement designs, the kind where a list is learned in one room and tested in another, gave d = .23, while interference-reduction designs gave .68 and multiple-context designs .45. An orienting task that made subjects relate list items to each other cut the effect to d = .13, 95% CI [.03, .23], against .33, 95% CI [.20, .46] for item-by-item processing. A retention interval of one day to one week gave d = .63, 95% CI [.42, .84], against .28 or less at each of the three shorter intervals coded. Changing the experimenter along with the room raised the effect from .26 to .62. Eighteen of the 93 effect sizes were above .80. The drug literature turns on the same cue logic, and Eich's 1980 review is where it was worked out. He compiled 27 studies yielding 57 cases, published or presented between January 1965 and December 1978, and sorted 50 of them by the kind of retrieval cue the rememberer had. Where retrieval was guided by invisible cues, as in free recall, 23 cases showed state dependence and 3 did not. Where list cues such as category names were supplied, 1 did and 10 did not. Where copy cues were, as in recognition, 2 did and 11 did not. Eich and Metcalfe ran four experiments using music to shift mood and the generate-read procedure to separate internally produced from externally presented items. Recall of generated items suffered more from a mood shift than recall of read items, and a shift in mood, arousal or both "did not deter recognition of either the occurrence or the origin of a target item". Pooling the recall data of all four studies, subjects whose mood changed a lot while their arousal changed little recalled fewer generated items than subjects matched on both, F(1, 189) = 5.07, p < .05, and fewer read items, F(1, 189) = 5.07, p < .05.

replication.headline: Smith and Vela's 93 effect sizes give a reliable but small d = .28, and the diving study that made the idea famous failed to replicate in 2021.
replication.detail: The meta-analytic answer and the direct-replication answer point in different directions, which is the whole story of this effect. Smith and Vela found environmental context effects reliable across 93 effect sizes, with free recall at d = .29, 95% CI [.21, .37]. Against that, Murre ran a replication of the diving study at Royal Society Open Science, which gave it results-blind in-principle acceptance; the OSF preregistration of the accepted Stage 1 manuscript was posted after data analysis, and Murre says so. He also records that no replication of the 1975 study had been published before his. Sixteen divers from Amsterdam clubs heard 36-word Dutch lists on land or underwater in a heated indoor pool, recalled them four minutes later in the same or the other place, and did all four combinations in one day rather than four. The interaction was not significant, F = 1.999, df1 = 1, df2 = 60, p = 0.163. Words learned underwater were recalled better on land than underwater, p < 0.01, which is the opposite of the predicted direction. A 2022 addendum matters and is usually not mentioned. Sean Mackinnon, working from Murre's posted data, found the analysis should have been a repeated-measures ANOVA with order as a between-subjects covariate, which is what yields the (1, 12) degrees of freedom Godden and Baddeley report, and found one raw value entered as 14 that should have been 13. Reanalysed, the learn-by-recall interaction is significant at p = 0.017 and the three-way interaction with order at p = 0.045. Murre's conclusion did not change, because the significant pattern is the wrong pattern: the same-context cells should have been the high ones and they were not. Fernandez and Glenberg had already published eight experiments under the title "Changing environmental context does not reliably affect memory". Across the free-recall conditions of those eight, they counted a same-context advantage above 2 per cent in 6 comparisons, a different-context advantage above 2 per cent in 6, and a difference under 2 per cent in 11. Their Experiment 8 repeated Smith's 1979 method with more than double the subjects and had power of .94 to detect the effect Smith reported. Smith and Vela's appendix codes their eight effect sizes at +.12, +.15, -.31, -.19, +.34, -.46, -.09 and +.26. In the mood literature the failure came from the original author. Bower and Mayer tried to reproduce the mood-dependent retrieval reported in Experiment 3 of Bower, Monteiro and Gilligan (1978), using the same two-list interference design on 48 hypnotisable subjects of 52 run. Recall percentages in the 1978 experiment had averaged 70 when learning and testing moods matched and 46 when they did not. Nothing of that size returned. Percent retention of list 1 gave F(2, 45) = 1.71, p < .19, and of list 2 F(2, 45) = 2.05, p < .14. One composite measure, which added other-list and extra-list intrusions to correct recall, did show the effect, F(2, 45) = 4.68, p < .01, and Bower and Mayer report it and set it aside: there was no mood-dependent effect "when the simplest, most direct, measures were used". Their conclusion was that mood-dependent retrieval "must be judged to be an unreliable phenomenon in the laboratory".

study.cite: Smith, S. M., & Vela, E. (2001). Environmental context-dependent memory: A review and meta-analysis. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 8(2), 203-220.

limits: The number in the `original` field is not Godden and Baddeley's own. It is Smith and Vela's coding of their study, and the condition means the 1975 paper prints are given above instead. The pooled d = .28 covers environmental context only. Smith and Vela excluded internal mood and pharmacological manipulations by design, as falling outside extrinsic context, so nothing in that figure speaks to state or mood dependence. They also excluded classroom reinstatement studies, on the ground that students are free to study outside the classroom and the study context is therefore uncontrolled. That exclusion is the direct answer to the revision advice built on this effect. Saufley, Otaka and Bavaresco tested the advice in real university courses and found no reliable effect in 21 comparisons across seven courses, with the direction of the mean differences inconsistent. Their design was thin where it mattered. The first midterm of their Experiment 1 put 16 students of 253 in a changed room against 237 in the lecture room, and the changed group scored 55.19 against 54.84. Seddon, reviewing the same paper, calls comparisons of that shape underpowered. Three sources could not be obtained on 21 September 2026. Godden and Baddeley's 1980 recognition paper, Ucros's mood-dependence meta-analysis and Eich's 1995 review are all closed at their publishers, with no repository copy listed by Unpaywall, Crossref, OpenAlex or Semantic Scholar; the publisher pages at Wiley, Taylor & Francis and Sage return a Cloudflare bot challenge rather than a paywall, so another reader may get further. The 1980 result quoted here is from the abstract Crossref carries. No pooled effect size from Ucros is quoted anywhere on this page. No multi-site or registered replication of any of the three literatures was located beyond Murre's single-laboratory diving replication and its addendum, in searches of PubMed, Crossref, OpenAlex and the open web on 21 September 2026. Effects of this size are hard to detect. Sixteen divers was enough only because the original estimate was enormous, and Murre says so.
misreadings: The diving study is quoted everywhere and its own sequel almost nowhere. Godden and Baddeley tested recognition five years later and found nothing, and any account that reports the 1975 crossover without the 1980 null has left out the finding that bounds it. The bound is real in direct comparisons and not visible in the aggregate, and both halves are true at once. Smith and Vela found no reliable difference by test type, Q_B = .21, with recall at .29, recognition at .27 and cued recall at .25. Their explanation is that the experiments comparing recall and recognition head to head all used word lists, which are highly associable, while the studies that do find context-dependent recognition used less associable material such as faces of incidentally encountered confederates. The advice to revise in the room you will be examined in does not follow from the meta-analysis. Reinstatement designs, which are the ones that model the advice, give the smallest effect of the three paradigms at d = .23, and the largest effects sit in interference-reduction designs that no student is running. Imagining the learning room worked about as well as returning to it, d = .26 against .28, so the practical recommendation the evidence supports is mental, not logistical. The word "state" also gets stretched. Mood-dependent memory, where a mood at learning cues retrieval regardless of what was learned, is not mood-congruent memory, where sad material is easier to recall while sad, and which has its own entry here. Eich and Metcalfe quote Blaney's reading of Weingartner and colleagues as a result that can be taken either way. A last one concerns the experimenter. Studies that changed the person running the session along with the room reported d = .62 against .26 for those that did not, so some of what is filed as environmental context is social.
